words.definition: Great generosity, especially shown through lavish gifts of money.
words.example: The library's new wing was funded entirely by the munificence of a single anonymous donor.
words.mnemonic: MUNI (money, as in a city's MUNIcipal budget) + -ficence — money handed out freely to the public.

words.definition: Nobility of spirit shown by being forgiving or generous, especially toward rivals.
words.example: In victory he showed remarkable magnanimity, publicly praising the opponent he had just defeated.
words.mnemonic: MAGNA (great) + ANIM (soul) — a 'great soul' too big to stoop to pettiness.

words.definition: Actively doing good and bringing kindness or help to others.
words.example: The beneficent king lowered taxes and built shelters for the city's poor.
words.mnemonic: BENE (good) + FIC (do) — one who DOes GOOD.

words.definition: The quality or act of doing good and showing active kindness.
words.example: The foundation's beneficence reached thousands of families in the weeks after the flood.
words.mnemonic: BENE (good) + -ence — the state of good-doing; picture a 'benefit' with the good spilling out.

words.definition: A kind, well-meaning disposition and the wish to help others.
words.example: She treated her employees with such benevolence that none of them ever wished to leave.
words.mnemonic: BENE (good) + VOL (wish, as in 'volition') — to WISH someone WELL.

words.definition: Selfless concern for the welfare of other people rather than oneself.
words.example: Donating a kidney to a stranger is an extraordinary act of altruism.
words.mnemonic: ALTRU- sounds like 'ALTER' (other) — always putting OTHERS first.

words.definition: The practice of helping others, especially by giving money to good causes.
words.example: After selling his company, he devoted his fortune to philanthropy, endowing schools around the world.
words.mnemonic: PHIL (love) + ANTHROPO (humankind) — LOVE of HUMANITY.

words.definition: Relating to or marked by generous efforts to improve the lives of others.
words.example: The philanthropic trust funds hospitals in regions that have no medical care at all.
words.mnemonic: PHIL (love) + ANTHROPO (human) — describing work driven by love of people.

words.definition: A wealthy person who gives generously to help others and worthy causes.
words.example: The hospital wing bears the name of the philanthropist who quietly paid for it.
words.mnemonic: PHIL (love) + ANTHROPO (human) + -IST — a PERSON who LOVES humankind.

words.definition: Existing or provided in large, plentiful amounts.
words.example: The autumn harvest was so bountiful that the barns could not hold it all.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'BOUNTY-full' — a pirate's chest crammed FULL of treasure.

words.definition: Supplied or given in generous, plentiful measure.
words.example: The host laid out a bounteous spread of meats, breads, and fruits for his guests.
words.mnemonic: 'BOUNTE-us' — bounty poured out onto US in overflowing measure.

words.definition: A generous supply of something, or a reward offered for a specific act.
words.example: The travelers marveled at the bounty of fresh fish the coastal village set before them.
words.mnemonic: From Latin BONITAS (goodness) — think 'BON' (good), as in 'bon appétit': good things aplenty.

words.definition: The quality of giving freely and being open-handed or broad-minded.
words.example: Her liberality knew no limits; she tipped waiters double and lent money to near strangers.
words.mnemonic: LIBER- means 'free' (Latin liber) — giving with a FREE hand.

words.definition: Given generously and without limit or holding back.
words.example: The coach offered unstinting praise, lifting up every player even after the loss.
words.mnemonic: UN + STINT — a 'stint' means to skimp or ration, so UN-stinting is NOT skimping.

words.definition: Spending money or resources recklessly and wastefully.
words.example: His prodigal habits emptied the entire inheritance within a single year.
words.mnemonic: Recall the biblical 'PRODIGAL son' who squandered his father's fortune.

words.definition: Available or existing in large amounts; more than what is needed.
words.example: After the heavy rains, mushrooms were plentiful across the damp forest floor.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'plenty-full' — picture a basket plenty full of apples.

words.definition: A great fullness or a large supply of something.
words.example: The new library offered a plenitude of rare manuscripts to eager scholars.
words.mnemonic: 'Plenty' + 'altitude' — a mountain-high stack of plenty.

words.definition: Existing in generous, ample supply; more than sufficient.
words.example: The harvest was so plenteous that farmers gave whole sacks of grain away.
words.mnemonic: 'Plenty-ous' — a table so full of plenty it groans under the food.

words.definition: A very large quantity of something; more than enough.
words.example: In spring the meadow shows an abundance of wildflowers in every color.
words.mnemonic: Picture 'a bun dance' — so many buns they dance across the table.

words.definition: Present in great quantity; more than adequate.
words.example: Fish were so abundant in the lake that every angler filled a bucket.
words.mnemonic: 'A bun-dant' — a bakery so stuffed the buns spill onto the floor.

words.definition: Great wealth shown through expensive, luxurious surroundings.
words.example: The palace's gold ceilings and marble floors spoke of staggering opulence.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'opal' — rooms glittering with opals and jewels.

words.definition: Splendid, costly, and impressive in a rich, luxurious way.
words.example: Guests marveled at the sumptuous banquet of roast meats, silks, and silver.
words.mnemonic: 'Sump-tuous' echoes 'consume' — a feast you long to consume.

words.definition: A symbol or supply overflowing with food and good things.
words.example: The market stall was a cornucopia of peaches, plums, figs, and grapes.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'cornu' (horn) + 'copia' (plenty): the horn of plenty.

words.definition: An amount beyond what is needed or useful; excess.
words.example: The essay drowned in a superfluity of adjectives that added nothing.
words.mnemonic: 'Super' + 'fluid' — water overflowing far past the brim.

words.definition: Beyond what is needed; extra and not required.
words.example: With the room already spotless, a second cleaning felt entirely superfluous.
words.mnemonic: 'Super-flu-ous' — a super flood of stuff you simply don't need.

words.definition: To give something, especially an honor or gift, to someone.
words.example: The queen chose to bestow a knighthood upon the loyal soldier.
words.mnemonic: 'Be' + 'stow' — to stow a gift into someone's keeping.

words.definition: To provide someone or something with money, property, or a quality.
words.example: A wealthy alumnus chose to endow the college with a new science wing.
words.mnemonic: 'En' + 'dow(ry)' — like a dowry, wealth given to set someone up.

words.definition: To leave money or possessions to someone through a will after death.
words.example: In her will, she chose to bequeath the farmhouse to her youngest niece.
words.mnemonic: 'Be-queath' sounds like 'beneath' — what you leave beneath you when you pass on.

words.definition: Money or property left to someone by a will.
words.example: The museum's finest painting arrived as a bequest from a late collector.
words.mnemonic: 'Be' + 'quest' — the treasure waiting at the end of a will's quest.

words.definition: A person who gives money or help to a cause, institution, or individual.
words.example: An anonymous benefactor quietly paid the tuition of every student in the class.
words.mnemonic: 'Bene' (good) + 'factor' (doer): a doer of good deeds.

words.definition: A gift of money or help given to a person or cause in need.
words.example: The library's new wing was funded entirely by a single anonymous benefaction.
words.mnemonic: bene- means 'good' (Latin) + faction sounds like 'action' — a good action done for others.

words.definition: A person who receives money, property, or advantages from something.
words.example: As the sole beneficiary of the will, she inherited the entire estate.
words.mnemonic: bene- 'good' + -ficiary — the one for whom the good is done.

words.definition: A person who gives financial or other support to an artist, charity, or shop.
words.example: The struggling painter finally found a wealthy patron to fund his studio.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'pater' (father) — a fatherly protector who backs you.

words.definition: The financial support or regular business given by a supporter or customer.
words.example: The café thrived thanks to the loyal patronage of the whole neighborhood.
words.mnemonic: 'Patron' + '-age' — the state or act of being a patron.

words.definition: To grant an honor, right, or benefit to someone.
words.example: The university will confer an honorary degree on the retiring scientist.
words.mnemonic: Latin con- 'together' + ferre 'to carry' — you carry something over and give it.

words.definition: To hand out or distribute something to people.
words.example: The pharmacist will dispense the medication once the prescription is verified.
words.mnemonic: dis- 'apart' + pense 'to weigh' (like 'pension') — to weigh out and give apart.

words.definition: To pay out money, especially from a fund.
words.example: The treasurer will disburse the grant funds to each department next week.
words.mnemonic: dis- + 'burse' (a purse, as in 'bursar') — money taken out of the purse.

words.definition: To assign or give a portion of something for a particular purpose.
words.example: Each speaker was allotted ten minutes to present their case.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'a lot' — you hand someone their lot, their fixed share.

words.definition: To set aside or assign resources for a specific purpose.
words.example: The committee decided to allocate most of the budget to road repairs.
words.mnemonic: al- + 'locate' — to give a resource its place or location.

words.definition: To divide and give out in fair or proper shares.
words.example: The judge had to apportion the blame between the two careless drivers.
words.mnemonic: a- + 'portion' — to hand each party its portion.

words.definition: To give out small portions of something, usually slowly or reluctantly.
words.example: The camp cook would dole out one thin ladle of soup to each child in line.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'doll' — picture handing out one tiny doll at a time to a long queue.

words.definition: To hand out or assign something, especially punishment or reward, by measured amounts.
words.example: The judge will mete out a harsher sentence to repeat offenders.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'meter' — a meter measures precisely, and to mete is to deal out by measure.

words.definition: A person who gives money, goods, or help to a cause or another person.
words.example: A generous donor covered the entire cost of the children's surgeries.
words.mnemonic: From Latin donare 'to give' — the same root as 'donate'.

words.definition: A small sum of money given for a service, beyond the required payment.
words.example: The waiter's attentive service earned him a generous gratuity.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'gratitude' — money handed over out of thanks.

words.definition: A sudden source of great wealth, luck, or success.
words.example: The newly discovered oil field proved to be a bonanza for the small town.
words.mnemonic: Spanish for 'fair weather, prosperity' — sounds like 'bonus' + 'nirvana', a jackpot.

words.definition: An unexpected sum of money or benefit that arrives by luck.
words.example: When the old stock finally soared, the sudden profit was a windfall the family never planned for.
words.mnemonic: Wind blows apples that FALL from the tree — free fruit you never worked for.

words.definition: Having plenty of money and a comfortable, prosperous standard of living.
words.example: They moved into an affluent suburb where every house had a gate, a pool, and a private drive.
words.mnemonic: Hidden 'flu' from Latin 'fluere' (to flow) — money flows toward the rich.

words.definition: The state of having an abundance of money and material comfort.
words.example: The marble floors and live-in chef were unmistakable signs of the family's affluence.
words.mnemonic: Root 'fluere' = to flow; picture cash flowing in until it pools around you.

words.definition: Growing thick, green, and healthy, or richly abundant and pleasing.
words.example: After a week of rain, the hillside turned lush with tall grass and wildflowers.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'plush' — soft, rich, thick, and deep, like a plush carpet of green.

words.definition: Growing thickly and abundantly; rich, dense, and profuse.
words.example: Her luxuriant hair spilled in thick, glossy waves all the way down her back.
words.mnemonic: Think 'luxury' for plants — greenery living large, overflowing with growth.

words.definition: The quality of growing thickly, richly, and in great abundance.
words.example: The jungle's luxuriance was so dense we couldn't see more than a few feet ahead.
words.mnemonic: Luxury plus abundance of growth — every leaf and vine overflowing.

words.definition: Filled to overflowing with moving people, animals, or things.
words.example: The tide pool was teeming with tiny crabs, snails, and darting silver fish.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'teaming' — everything crowded together in huge, swarming teams.

words.definition: Fully filled or generously supplied with something.
words.example: The old library was replete with rare maps, first editions, and dusty atlases.
words.mnemonic: Re + 'plete' (Latin 'plere', to fill), like 'complete' — filled right up.

words.definition: To soak something completely or fill it beyond any more capacity.
words.example: The downpour quickly saturated the soil until puddles pooled across the whole yard.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'satur' = full; a long 'Saturday' soak leaves you dripping wet.

words.definition: To flood with water, or to overwhelm with a huge quantity of things.
words.example: After the offer went live, the support team was inundated with thousands of emails.
words.mnemonic: Latin 'unda' = wave; hear 'in-UNDA-ate' as waves rolling in to flood the shore.

words.definition: To satisfy an appetite or desire completely, sometimes to excess.
words.example: The enormous holiday feast satiated even the hungriest guests around the table.
words.mnemonic: Root 'satis' = enough; you've had enough — and then a little too much.

words.definition: To fully satisfy a hunger, thirst, or craving.
words.example: A tall glass of cold water was all it took to sate her thirst after the long run.
words.mnemonic: 'Sate' = you 'sat' back, fully fed, unable to take another bite.

words.definition: To eat greedily until completely stuffed.
words.example: The children gorged on cake and candy until they could barely move from the couch.
words.mnemonic: Picture cramming food down your 'gorge' (throat) until it bulges.

words.definition: To sicken or weary someone through too much sweetness or excess.
words.example: The frosting was so sugary that the cupcake began to cloy after just two bites.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'clog' — too much sweetness clogs your throat and turns your stomach.

words.definition: An amount left over after all needs have been fully met.
words.example: The harvest was so good that the farm sold its grain surplus to neighboring towns.
words.mnemonic: 'Sur' (over) + 'plus' — a plus that spills over the top: extra to spare.

words.definition: Spending money or resources recklessly and wastefully, with no thought for the future.
words.example: The heir burned through his inheritance in two years with profligate spending on yachts and parties.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like "pro-fli-gate" — imagine a rich guy flinging money out an open gate, letting it all fly away.

words.definition: The state of squandering money or living with reckless moral abandon.
words.example: Historians blame the empire's collapse on decades of court profligacy and empty treasuries.
words.mnemonic: The '-acy' turns the wasteful person into the habit itself — like 'privacy' is the state of being private, this is the state of a spendthrift.

words.definition: Spending or costing far more than is reasonable or necessary.
words.example: She threw an extravagant party with imported orchids in every corner and a live orchestra.
words.mnemonic: Extra + vagant (Latin vagari, 'to wander') — your spending wanders EXTRA far beyond the budget.

words.definition: Excessive spending, or a costly luxury beyond what one needs.
words.example: A weekend at the spa felt like a rare extravagance for someone who usually clipped coupons.
words.mnemonic: The noun of 'extravagant' — the wandering EXTRA far is now the act itself, an -ance you can point to.

words.definition: Done without good reason, or given free of charge; uncalled for and unwarranted.
words.example: The film's gratuitous violence added nothing to the plot and left viewers uneasy.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'gratis' (free) — something thrown in for free, and by extension, uncalled for.

words.definition: Extreme unwillingness to spend money or use resources.
words.example: His parsimony was legendary: he reused tea bags and washed disposable forks.
words.mnemonic: 'Parse-money' — someone who parses every single coin before letting it go.

words.definition: Hoarding wealth and hating to part with even small amounts.
words.example: Their miserly landlord refused to fix the heater to save a few dollars in winter.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'miser' — picture Scrooge hunhappily clutching his coins, MISERable because he won't spend.

words.definition: Grudgingly giving or spending as little as possible.
words.example: The boss handed out niggardly bonuses that barely covered a single dinner.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'niggling' — a niggling, pinching reluctance to give a decent amount.

words.definition: The state of being extremely poor; severe lack of money.
words.example: After the mill closed, the family slipped into penury, pawning heirlooms just to eat.
words.mnemonic: 'Penny-ury' — when all you have left is pennies. Penny + misery.

words.definition: Careful, economical management of money and resources.
words.example: Through years of quiet thrift, she saved enough to retire at fifty.
words.mnemonic: Same root as 'thrive' — managing money carefully lets you THRIVE later.

words.definition: Managing money and resources carefully to avoid waste.
words.example: The thrifty student cooked at home all week so he could afford one trip abroad.
words.mnemonic: The '-y' makes a person out of 'thrift' — someone who THRIVES by not wasting.

words.definition: Unwilling to give or spend, even when able to.
words.example: He was so stingy he split the restaurant bill down to the last shared french fry.
words.mnemonic: A 'sting' — parting with money stings so much you refuse to do it.

words.definition: A person who hates spending and hoards every coin.
words.example: The office skinflint drove across town to save four cents a gallon on gas.
words.mnemonic: Skin + flint — a person so cheap he'd 'skin a flint' (scrape a stone) for a scrap of value.

words.definition: An extreme, grasping desire for wealth or gain.
words.example: Blinded by avarice, the banker gambled his clients' savings on a doomed scheme.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'a-VOR-ice' — think 'devour' — a hunger that devours, always craving more gold.

words.definition: Driven by an extreme, grasping hunger for money or gain.
words.example: The avaricious developer bulldozed the park to squeeze in a few more luxury condos.
words.mnemonic: The adjective of 'avarice' — like 'delicious' but for greed: someone who finds money too DELICIOUS to resist.

words.definition: An intense, selfish craving for money or material possessions.
words.example: The heirs' cupidity turned the reading of the will into a shouting match.
words.mnemonic: Cupid + ity — but this Cupid shoots arrows of greed, aiming for gold instead of love.

words.definition: Filled with an envious longing for what belongs to someone else.
words.example: She cast a covetous glance at her neighbor's gleaming new car.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'cover-us' — you want to cover yourself in everyone else's belongings.

words.definition: To wish enviously to own something that belongs to another person.
words.example: Thou shalt not covet — yet he still eyed his brother's inheritance daily.
words.mnemonic: Covet sounds like 'covered' — you crave what's hidden under someone else's cover.

words.definition: Aggressively greedy and eager to seize as much as possible.
words.example: The rapacious landlord raised rents until half the tenants were forced to flee.
words.mnemonic: Think of a raptor — a bird of prey — swooping down to snatch everything in its talons (same Latin root, rapere, to seize).

words.definition: The quality of being aggressively greedy and grasping for more.
words.example: The empire's rapacity stripped its colonies of gold, timber, and dignity.
words.mnemonic: Rapt + capacity: an endless capacity to snatch (from Latin rapere, to seize).

words.definition: Selfishly eager to acquire money or things, often at others' expense.
words.example: Her grasping business partner tried to claim every last cent of the profits.
words.mnemonic: Picture hands literally clutching at money and refusing to let go — grasping.

words.definition: Willing to act dishonestly or be bribed in exchange for money.
words.example: The venal inspector waved the safety violations through once cash changed hands.
words.mnemonic: Think 'vend' — everything is for sale, even the official's integrity. (Don't confuse with 'venial,' a minor sin.)

words.definition: To gather and secretly store a large supply, keeping it from others.
words.example: During the shortage, panicked shoppers began to hoard flour and bottled water.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'horde' — a huge horde of stuff piled up, the way a dragon guards its treasure.

words.definition: To spend very little and economize severely, often on necessities.
words.example: They scrimped for years, skipping vacations and dinners out, to afford a home.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'skimp' and 'shrimp' — you shrink your spending down to shrimp size.

words.definition: To supply or use something in an ungenerously small amount.
words.example: A great teacher, she never stinted on praise when her students worked hard.
words.mnemonic: Stint is 'stingy' with the ending clipped off — a stingy person always stints.

words.definition: To deliberately keep back or refuse to give something wanted or owed.
words.example: The company chose to withhold the bonuses until the audit was complete.
words.mnemonic: With + hold: you keep it 'with' you and 'hold' onto it instead of handing it over.

words.definition: Very small in amount and not enough to satisfy a need.
words.example: The refugees survived for weeks on a meager ration of rice and water.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'meek + eager' — too meek to ask for more, so you stay hungry and eager.

words.definition: Too small or too few to be adequate.
words.example: The prosecution's case rested on scanty evidence and quickly fell apart.
words.mnemonic: Scant + y — and 'scant' means barely any; a scanty outfit barely covers anything.

words.definition: So small or trivial as to be worthless or insulting.
words.example: After a year of overtime, the paltry raise felt like a slap in the face.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'poultry' — a scrawny little chicken hardly worth the trouble of eating.

words.definition: Marked by strict simplicity, self-discipline, and the absence of luxury.
words.example: The monastery's spartan cells held only a cot, a candle, and a worn bible.
words.mnemonic: The ancient warriors of Sparta lived hard, disciplined lives with zero comforts — hence spartan.

description: mid-frequency and academic register — generosity and stinginess
